title: Episode 188: Jimmy Carter: The Peanut Farmer, the Nuclear Core, and Camp David (1924–1978)
description:
James Earl Carter Jr. was the quintessential outsider: a devout Southern Baptist peanut farmer from Plains, Georgia, who graduated from the United States Naval Academy and helped build America's nuclear submarine fleet under the legendary Admiral Hyman Rickover. In 1952, Lieutenant Carter displayed extraordinary physical courage when he led a team into the contaminated radioactive core of a melting nuclear reactor at Chalk River, Canada, absorbing dangerous radiation in ninety-second shifts to save the facility. Running for president in 1976 carrying his own luggage and promising 'I'll never tell a lie,' Carter captured the nation's heart in the wake of Watergate. On Inauguration Day in 1977, he stunned security by walking the entire mile down Pennsylvania Avenue hand-in-hand with Rosalynn. In September 1978, Carter achieved his greatest diplomatic triumph, locking Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin inside Camp David for thirteen grueling days to broker a historic peace treaty that has endured for generations. Discover the unshakeable moral conviction of America's thirty-ninth president.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the principled, humble world of Jimmy Carter. With Carter, the White House welcomed a leader who carried his own garment bags, wore cardigan sweaters, installed solar panels, and possessed an iron moral spine. Here is George with the story of the peanut farmer from Plains, the Canadian nuclear reactor hero, and the miracle of the Camp David Accords.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE RED DIRT OF PLAINS AND NAVAL DISCIPLINE
James Earl Carter Jr. was born in October 1924 in Plains, Georgia—the first American president born in a hospital. He grew up on a farm in nearby Archery, where his family's wooden home possessed neither electricity nor indoor plumbing until his teenage years. Young 'Jimmy' rose before dawn to haul water, chop firewood, and work the red-clay peanut fields beside African American tenant farmers, developing a deep, lifelong reverence for racial equality from his mother, Lillian Carter, a beloved registered nurse who routinely provided free medical care to poor Black families in defiance of local Jim Crow customs. A brilliant, disciplined student who read encyclopedias for pleasure, Carter realized his childhood dream in 1943 by securing an appointment to the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis. Graduating in the top ten percent of the Class of 1946, Carter married his hometown sweetheart, Rosalynn Smith—an ambitious, sharp-minded young woman who would become his indispensable intellectual equal and political partner for seventy-seven years. Commissioned as an ensign, Carter volunteered for the submarine service, serving aboard diesel boats in the Atlantic and Pacific before catching the eye of a legendary naval pioneer: Captain Hyman G. Rickover. The austere values of the Georgia red dirt gave Jimmy Carter an authentic, unpretentious grounding in the daily struggles of ordinary working people that never faded throughout his life. The red clay of Georgia taught Carter that integrity, labor, and faith are the bedrock of human dignity, guiding his actions in public and private life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: ADMIRAL RICKOVER AND THE MELTDOWN AT CHALK RIVER
In 1948, Carter was hand-picked by Admiral Hyman G. Rickover—the brilliant, tyrannical father of the nuclear navy—to join the elite team developing the world's first nuclear-powered submarines. During his entrance interview, Rickover subjected young Carter to an intense, two-hour psychological grilling on music, literature, and naval engineering. Finally, Rickover asked Carter how he had ranked at Annapolis. Carter puffed out his chest and answered proudly: 'Fifty-ninth in a class of eight hundred and twenty, sir.' Rickover stared coldly and asked: 'Did you always do your best?' Carter hesitated, thought of the hours he had slacked off, and truthfully replied: 'No, sir, not always.' Rickover leaned forward and asked a question that echoed through Carter's conscience for the rest of his life: 'Why not?' Carter later chose that phrase for his bestselling autobiography: 'Why Not the Best?' In December 1952, Carter's scientific training was put to the ultimate test when the NRX experimental nuclear reactor at Chalk River, Ontario, suffered a partial meltdown. Lieutenant Carter led a twenty-three-man team to disassemble the radioactive core. Lowered into the ruptured core in ninety-second shifts wearing lead-lined suits, Carter absorbed high doses of radiation to manually turn wrenches, saving the reactor. That harrowing ninety-second shift inside the melting Canadian reactor demonstrated Carter's rare combination of scientific mastery, iron physical courage, and selflessness. Rickover's demanding standards instilled in Carter a perfectionist's devotion to detail, governance, and moral responsibility.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: RETURNING TO PLAINS AND THE GOVERNOR'S MANSION
In 1953, following the death of his father, Carter made a decision that astonished his naval peers: he resigned his promising naval commission, surrendered his dreams of high command, and returned home to Plains to take over the family's struggling peanut and fertilizer warehouse. Living in public housing for a year, Jimmy and Rosalynn worked grueling fourteen-hour days, turning the enterprise into a highly prosperous agribusiness. Entering local politics, Carter won election to the Georgia State Senate, where he was a solitary voice against segregationist intimidation. In 1970, after an unsuccessful first attempt, Carter was elected Governor of Georgia. At his inaugural address on the steps of the state capitol in January 1971, the quiet peanut farmer stunned the political establishment of the Deep South by boldly proclaiming: 'I say to you quite frankly that the time for racial discrimination is over.' Carter hung portraits of Martin Luther King Jr. in the capitol, integrated state regulatory boards, reorganized state government into streamlined departments, and landed on the cover of Time magazine as the champion of the progressive 'New South.' His courageous inaugural declaration against racial discrimination in Georgia established Carter as the vanguard of a progressive New South that embraced equality and justice. His bold declaration that the era of segregation was over broke decades of regional political silence, setting a new moral standard for southern leadership.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: 'JIMMY WHO?' AND THE 1976 PRESIDENTIAL MIRACLE
In December 1974, Jimmy Carter announced he was running for President of the United States. The reaction of the national press was derisive laughter; the Atlanta Constitution ran a famous headline asking: 'Jimmy Who is Running for What?' In an era before modern cable television, Carter understood the primary calendar better than the party bosses. With his mother, Miss Lillian, his wife, Rosalynn, and his sons, Carter launched an unprecedented, two-year grassroots campaign across Iowa and New Hampshire. Traveling on commercial airlines with his suits draped over his arm, Carter slept on couches in supporters' spare bedrooms, poured coffee in diner booths, and introduced himself with simple modesty: 'My name is Jimmy Carter, and I'm running for President.' In the wake of Vietnam and Watergate, his absolute moral earnestness captured the soul of an exhausted nation. His core campaign promise was unshakeable: 'I will never tell a lie to the American people.' In November 1976, Carter defeated incumbent Gerald Ford, becoming the first president from the Deep South elected since Zachary Taylor in 1848. Carter's grassroots victory proved that authentic honesty, personal warmth, and humble moral conviction could triumph over established political machines and insider conventional wisdom. His simple, straightforward campaign demonstrated that ordinary Americans longed for transparency, honesty, and genuine moral purpose in government.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE WALK DOWN PENNSYLVANIA AVENUE: JANUARY 1977
On January 20, 1977, following his swearing-in on the Capitol steps, President Jimmy Carter executed a dramatic symbolic break with the imperial presidency that electrified the world. As the presidential motorcade moved down Pennsylvania Avenue toward the White House, the black armored limousine suddenly slowed to a halt. The door swung open, and to the absolute horror of the Secret Service, Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter stepped out into the crisp winter air. Holding hands with their nine-year-old daughter Amy skipping between them, the Carters smiled, waved, and walked the entire mile-and-a-half to the executive mansion on foot, surrounded by cheering crowds. It was a breathtaking demonstration of democratic humility: the President was not a monarch secluded behind tinted bulletproof glass, but a citizen among citizens. Carter slashed White House limousines, sold the presidential yacht Sequoia, carried his own luggage aboard Air Force One, banned the playing of 'Hail to the Chief' at routine public appearances, and insisted on being addressed simply as 'Jimmy.' That iconic mile-and-a-half walk down Pennsylvania Avenue permanently redefined the symbolic relationship between the American chief executive and the citizens he serves. The mile-long walk down the avenue broke decades of executive aloofness, showing a leader who considered himself a humble servant of the people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: CARDIGANS, SOLAR PANELS, AND HUMAN RIGHTS
Carter brought an austere, forward-looking scientific vision to the presidency that was decades ahead of its time. In February 1977, facing a national winter fuel shortage, Carter sat in a cardigan sweater before a roaring fireplace in the Oval Office to deliver a televised chat on energy, urging Americans to conserve fuel, turn down their thermostats, and embrace renewable power. In 1979, he installed thirty-two solar hot-water panels on the roof of the West Wing, presciently declaring that solar energy could provide a clean, infinite supply of power for future generations. Carter created the Department of Energy, established the Department of Education, deregulated the airline and trucking industries to spur commercial competition and lower passenger fares, and enacted the landmark Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, protecting over one hundred million acres of pristine wilderness. In foreign policy, Carter established human rights as the supreme guiding principle of American diplomacy, cutting aid to brutal military dictatorships in Latin America and negotiating the controversial Panama Canal Treaties to return the canal to Panama. His forward-looking focus on renewable energy, environmental preservation, and international human rights positioned Carter decades ahead of his contemporary political peers. Carter's installation of solar panels and creation of the Energy Department laid the intellectual and policy foundations for the modern green energy transition.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE MIRACLE OF THE CAMP DAVID ACCORDS: 1978
Carter's crowning moment of diplomatic genius arrived in September 1978 at the presidential retreat at Camp David, Maryland. For thirty years, Egypt and Israel had fought four bloody, catastrophic wars, locked in an unbridgeable chasm of hatred. Carter took an immense personal gamble: he invited Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin to Camp David, cutting them off from press leaks and staff interference for thirteen exhausting days. When negotiations broke down and Begin packed his suitcases to leave on day eleven, Carter walked into Begin's cabin with a set of autographed photographs of the three leaders that Begin had requested for his grandchildren. Carter handed them to Begin, reading aloud the names of Begin's eight grandchildren: 'This one is for your granddaughter... and this for your grandson.' Begin looked at the photos, choked with tears, and realized that the future of those children hung upon his decision. Begin unpacked his bags. On September 17, 1978, in the East Room of the White House, Sadat and Begin signed the Camp David Accords, establishing a permanent, historic peace treaty between Egypt and Israel that has endured to this very day. The Camp David Accords stand as one of the most remarkable diplomatic achievements in world history, a testament to the power of relentless personal patience and moral courage. The Camp David Accords proved that even the most bitter, generational hatreds can be overcome through patient, principled diplomacy.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Jimmy Carter's triumph at Camp David proved the power of moral diplomacy and relentless personal patience. But his presidency was about to encounter a perfect storm of global crises: soaring inflation, gas lines, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and the harrowing capture of fifty-two American hostages in Tehran. Next week, we conclude our Jimmy Carter saga: the infamous 'Killer Rabbit' incident, the 444-day Iran Hostage Crisis, the disaster at Desert One, and his extraordinary four-decade post-presidency building homes with Habitat for Humanity and winning the Nobel Peace Prize. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
